description: We are a team from Uralsk, Kazakhstan, participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge and working on the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge.Our goal is to create an interactive Martian exploration and navigation tool that combines data from multiple NASA missions into a clear and practical map for future human explorers.
summary: Walkback Envelope is an interactive concept demonstrator for planning a Mars surface walk around one question: can the astronaut still walk back to the habitat? It combines real MOLA/HRSC terrain from four Martian regions with an assumed spacesuit budget for cooling water, carbon-dioxide removal, battery energy and oxygen. A directed terrain-cost field visualizes where the current inventory could support a return with a chosen reserve, while illustrative radiation and equipment-failure scenarios show additional constraints. Users can move a science target, change the site, and explore how time, walking pace and payload affect the result. The project addresses the Martian Map challenge by integrating topography, resource estimates and a historical radiation reference into one decision-oriented interface. The terrain is observed; habitats, shelters, capacities and scenarios are assumptions. This is an educational and exploratory prototype, not validated astronaut-safety software.
details: TEAM ORDINATUM — WALKBACK ENVELOPE THE IDEA A route to a science target is useful only if the crew can also return. Walking uphill and downhill has different modelled costs, and oxygen is not the only consumable. Our contribution is an interactive integration of terrain, four resource channels and an independent radiation warning, making these trade-offs visible rather than presenting distance alone. DATA AND WORKFLOW We extracted four 25 km terrain fragments around Jezero, Gale, Melas Chasma and Elysium Planitia from the USGS/NASA/DLR MOLA + HRSC blended digital elevation model (200 m source pixels), using GDAL remote reads. The working grid is 84 by 84, approximately 298 m per cell. NASA JPL Mars Trek, listed among this challenge's resources, supplies the context basemap. Historical Curiosity/MSL RAD measurements provide a radiation scale reference; they are not live space-weather observations. Apollo EVA averages are a scale reference for energy expenditure, not a matched calibration dataset. HOW IT WORKS A directed shortest-path search prices walking over the elevation grid. Uphill and downhill edges have different metabolic costs; model edges above 45 percent grade are excluded. The outbound route is searched over terrain, and a reverse cost field estimates return costs. Both use 16 travel directions. Four channel estimates track cooling water in kilograms, CO2 absorption capacity in grams, battery energy in watt-hours and oxygen in grams. Remaining inventory minus estimated return need is compared against a user-selected fraction of initial capacity, 25 percent by default. The green envelope represents this approximate resource condition, not overall safety. Dose and illustrative solar-event warnings are separate. USING THE DEMO Open the Project link in a modern browser; no account or installation is needed. Drag EVA ELAPSED, switch the four sites, or click the map to move the science target. Change pace, payload and reserve, and compare nominal, dust-storm, scrubber-failure and solar-event scenarios. The seven-slide English presentation is linked under Project Demonstration. A self-contained built HTML file is also available in the public repository for local use; the optional NASA Trek context tile needs internet access. WHAT IS ASSUMED AND WHAT IS NOT VALIDATED The habitats, science targets, safe havens, caches, suit capacities and weather scenarios are hypothetical. The metabolic model is a heuristic Mars-gravity adaptation of Pandolf, not validated suited-Mars physiology. At 1.7 km/h on level terrain it returns about 225.7 W, below our 300–500 W design target; higher real expenditure would reduce the resource envelope. The 3 mSv abort value, event multiplier and warning lead time are illustrative project settings, not NASA-approved medical limits or a demonstrated worst case. The horizon/sky-view radiation adjustment is geometric, not particle-transport modelling. Metre-scale boulders, cracks, fatigue and detailed suit dynamics are unresolved. IMPORTANT INTERPRETATION LIMITS The current-return verdict and whole-plan warning answer different questions; the whole-plan check remains incomplete. The current PNR display is a hypothetical outbound deadline, capped at the target, not a certified loss-of-return point on the executed plan. The simulation may return above reserve after this deadline. Haven forecasts still simplify cache depletion, suit capacity and stopping costs; their expanded zones are not proven executable safe-return paths. The simulated return and predicted cost-field route are not identical. These are explicit limitations, not safety guarantees. DEVELOPMENT AND VERIFICATION We used JavaScript modules and HTML Canvas, Python, GDAL, Node.js, Pillow and PyMuPDF; source code is publicly available under MIT. Regression tests and sampled invariant checks helped find implementation defects, but they do not validate physiology or certify all UI states. An earlier 288-configuration sweep had a pace-input error and must not be treated as comprehensive validation. The test suite also includes a separately labelled legacy suit-budget fixture and a declared metabolic deviation. AI ASSISTANCE Claude and OpenAI Codex assisted with ideation, research, code, model derivation, debugging, reviews, documentation, visual layout and presentation preparation. The team is responsible for the resulting decisions and claims. No live AI model is embedded in the application. Observed terrain data were not generated by AI. Map renderings and screenshots are produced by our AI-assisted visualization code; the slides and README disclose this assistance. No NASA logo is used as our branding. NEXT STEPS Use independently validated energy-expenditure inputs, propagate uncertainty, reconcile plan/PNR/return semantics and route costs, implement conserved capacity-limited resupply, and assess finer terrain and physically supported radiation models. PUBLIC SOURCE AND DOCUMENTATION https://github.com/ordinatum/walkback-envelope https://ordinatum.github.io/walkback-envelope/slides.html
